Every node on the GPU: local LLMs on Strix Halo in Lemonade

On a Ryzen AI Max+ 395 (Strix Halo), the 1bit engine now runs every graph node of every local LLM and mode we test on the integrated Radeon 8060S GPU, through AMD's HRX runtime and our own HIP kernels. Nothing falls back to the CPU. Here is what landed ahead of the first release, measured on that machine.

Update (2026-10-30): the release candidate's checks are green: the 1bit OS live image passes 17 of 17 checks on the board with Secure Boot on, and the hardware gate is green at the shipping pin; the tag and the packages are the owner's. The engine is pinned to Lemonade's weekly release. Current numbers: Models measured; status: Releases.

43 of 43 configurations, all on the GPU with HRX#

We keep a census of the models people run and the modes they run them in: a short chat, a long prompt, a q8 KV cache, four requests in parallel, speculative decoding with MTP, embeddings and reranking. The models are Qwen3 0.6B, 4B and 8B, Qwen3.8-27B, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, GLM-4.7-Flash, ZAYA1-8B, LFM2, MiniCPM, and the nomic, bge and jina embedding and reranking models.

On 20 October the census found 12 gaps, places where a node still ran on the CPU. All 12 are closed. The closing census: 43 of 43 runnable configurations with 0 nodes off the GPU, one graph split, and every request answered (how HRX runs; #476, #480, #481). Among them:

  • a q8_0 KV cache, with K and V or K alone, now keeps flash attention on the GPU;
  • four parallel requests work on LFM2, ZAYA1-8B and the Qwen3.5/3.8 family;
  • Qwen3.8-27B with MTP answers an 8K-token prompt;
  • jina-bert's attention, with its ALiBi bias, runs on the GPU.

Qwen3.8-27B speed with MTP speculative decoding#

Qwen3.8-27B (UD-Q4_K_XL) with MTP speculative decoding, greedy 256-token chats:

prompt before now
code 25.9 tok/s 36.0 tok/s
prose 20.5 tok/s 26.8 tok/s
short 21.9 tok/s 29.9 tok/s

The verify step checks four tokens at once. New kernels for 2 to 8 tokens took it from 121 ms to 88 ms (#487). Decode without MTP is unchanged at 12.2 tok/s. The same model reads a 4,096-token prompt at 560 to 585 tok/s, depending on the batch size (llama-bench). How to run it: 1bit serve.

Strict GPU placement by default#

A node that quietly runs on the CPU is a slowdown nobody asked for. HRX placement is now strict by default: if any node of a model would run on the CPU, the load stops with one line that names the node, its op and its shape, and --no-strict-device turns the fallback back on (#482).

The hardware gate that every pin change passes now builds our kernels into the server, checks that every graph of every gate model is on the GPU, adds q8 KV cache rows, and checks every kernel registration against its compiled code at startup (#478, #484). That gate caught three bugs this week before they reached main (the hardware gate).

The runtime also got safer: one memory budget for every buffer, coherent host reads, and after a GPU fault the server refuses new work and exits cleanly, so Lemonade can restart the model (#486).

Inside Lemonade, on Ubuntu 26.04 and as 1bit OS#

Lemonade now starts the engine's llama-server directly: one HTTP hop instead of two, one process fewer, and a quarter of a second off each model load (#475). On Ubuntu 26.04 the stock lemond from the Lemonade PPA can use the engine through a systemd drop-in, with no patch to Lemonade (#483). The same build also ships as the 1bit OS image, a bootable Lemonade appliance (the engine in Lemonade).

The NPU engine#

The XDNA 2 NPU engine is coming along: correctness first, speed next (NPU status). More in a later post.

When it ships#

The first release goes out when every item on our release checklist is done. Three full release rehearsals this week (build, packages, the OS image booted in a VM, a clean build from the binary drop) passed end to end (releases).
